bib.title: Learning to summarize from human feedback

read.skipped: References skimmed; sample Tables 24-29 skimmed, not recorded.

question: Can training a summarizer against a reward model learned from human pairwise comparisons beat supervised fine-tuning and human reference summaries?
hypothesis: Optimising a learned human-preference reward yields better summaries than maximum likelihood on references or optimising ROUGE.
contributions: Human feedback models significantly outperform strong baselines on English summarization, including 10x larger supervised models and the reference summaries
Human feedback models transfer to CNN/DM news without news-specific fine-tuning
Extensive analysis of the policy and reward model, including scaling and over-optimisation
Public release of 64,832 TL;DR comparisons and evaluation data

method.summary: Fine-tune GPT-3-style 1.3B and 6.7B models on filtered Reddit TL;DR, collect pairwise human comparisons in batches, train a reward model from the supervised model, then optimise the policy with PPO plus a KL penalty to the supervised model. Evaluate with human preference and Likert scores, with transfer to CNN/DM.

datasets.name: Reddit TL;DR (Volske et al. 2017), filtered
datasets.size: 123,169 posts with summaries, ~5% validation; 287,790 posts filtered by body only used for RL
datasets.split: ~5% held out; 1913 validation posts used for model selection and excluded from evaluations
datasets.preprocessing: Remove ~20,000 exact duplicates, top-level posts only, whitelist subreddits, drop Edit/Update titles and sensitive topics, drop posts with body >512 tokens; reference summaries kept only 24-48 tokens, profanity and Edit/Update/P.S. removed

datasets.name: Human comparison dataset (TL;DR)
datasets.size: 64,832 summary comparisons released; RM scaling uses 8k-64k
datasets.source: collected by Upwork, Scale and Lionbridge labelers
datasets.preprocessing: Labelers write naive interpretations, then give a 9-point confidence comparison; most comparisons have a single label

datasets.name: CNN/DailyMail
datasets.preprocessing: Transfer only, no news training for human-feedback models; outputs lower-cased and re-capitalised for fairness; one 6.7B supervised model also fine-tuned on it

models.name: GPT-3-style pretrained 1.3B/3B/6.7B/13B
models.init_from: pretrained on Commoncrawl, Webtext, books, Wikipedia

other.schedule: cosine with short warmup, decay to 10% of max

models.name: Reward model (rm4, rm4_6b)
models.architecture: supervised baseline plus randomly initialised linear scalar head, weights N(0,1/(d_model+1))

other.normalisation: outputs shifted so reference summaries have mean 0

models.name: PPO policy (sup4 ppo rm4, sup4_6b ppo rm4_6b)
models.architecture: as base; separate value network of the same size
models.init_from: supervised baseline; value function initialised from reward model

training.objective: Supervised: next-token on reference summaries. RM: pairwise logistic loss on human comparisons. Policy: PPO on R(x,y)=r_theta(x,y)-beta*log[pi_RL(y|x)/pi_SFT(y|x)], reward only at EOS, gamma=1
training.lr_schedule: cosine for supervised and RM; linear decay for PPO
training.epochs: Supervised 1 epoch; RM 1 epoch; PPO 4 epochs per batch of rollouts
training.precision: fp16 activations; fp32 weights except TL;DR supervised baselines (fp16 weights)
training.regularisation: KL penalty to SFT policy, coefficient 0.05 for both main runs; lambda=0.95 GAE
training.seeds: RM: sweep 3 to 10 seeds and pick best on development validation; lr from log-linear sweep of at least 7 values

other.RM_selection: best on development portion of validation set filtered to high-confidence labels
other.pipeline: offline batch setting; each RM trained on all labels collected so far

inference.decoding: T=0 for all final human evaluations
inference.temperature: 0 (final evals); 0.7 for best-of-N sampling and agreement tables; 0.3 for CNN/DM supervised
inference.top_p: Nucleus sampling tried and found worse than very low temperature (Fig 8)
inference.max_tokens: summaries under 48 tokens; input max 512 tokens (1999 for pretrained with few-shot context)
inference.samples: Best-of-N up to N=2048 from the 1.3B supervised baseline

parameters.KL_coefficient: 0.05 main runs; 0.35 to 0.05 swept in Table 9

metrics.name: Preference over reference summaries
metrics.definition: fraction of a policy's summaries humans prefer to the dataset reference summary

metrics.name: Likert quality
metrics.definition: 1-7 scores on coverage, accuracy, coherence, overall

metrics.name: RM validation accuracy / agreement
metrics.definition: fraction of human comparisons the RM (or metric) agrees with

eval.protocol: Hired labelers (Upwork, Scale, Lionbridge); error bars are 1 standard error; agreement with researchers monitored; 1913 validation posts excluded from evaluation.

availability.code: inference code for the 1.3B models and baselines released (link not in text)

evidence.quote: We used a KL coefﬁcient of 0.05 for both of the main runs

results.claim: A 1.3B human-feedback policy beats a 10x larger supervised policy on preference against reference summaries.
results.metric: fraction of summaries preferred over reference
results.setup: TL;DR (filtered Reddit), human pairwise or Likert evaluation, T=0 sampling for final evaluations; 1.3B PPO vs 6.7B supervised
results.quote: 61% versus 43% raw preference score against reference summaries

results.claim: After controlling for length the 6.7B human-feedback model is still preferred to reference summaries.
results.setup: TL;DR (filtered Reddit), human pairwise or Likert evaluation, T=0 sampling for final evaluations; 6.7B PPO; logistic regression on policy id and log length ratio (App F)
results.note: Text says preference drops by ~5% after length control.
results.quote: preferred to the reference summaries ~65% of the time

results.claim: 6.7B PPO summaries get a perfect 7/7 overall score far more often than supervised or reference.
results.setup: TL;DR (filtered Reddit), human pairwise or Likert evaluation, T=0 sampling for final evaluations; 7-point Likert; 6.7B PPO vs 6.7B supervised (20%) and reference (23%)
results.quote: overall score 45% of the time (compared to 20% and 23%

limits: No baseline of supervised fine-tuning on an equal amount of high-quality human demonstrations (too expensive, App D)
Roughly two thirds of TL;DR is relationship posts, a narrow domain
RL for 6.7B cost ~320 GPU-days and labels took thousands of labeler hours
Supervised TL;DR baselines used fp16 weights while RL used fp32, a small unfixed discrepancy (footnote 11)
Over-optimising the RM makes it anti-correlated with human preference; RM biased toward longer summaries
Labeler pool skews White and American; data collection was exploratory and unsystematic (App C.6)
CNN/DM reference summaries (highlights) are questionable references
